touches.text: superclaude is Python on every box, launched by the platform shell (5.4.3.8.5), and inherits the elevation the shell settled (5.4.3.8.6): elevated PowerShell on Windows, sudo with IS_SANDBOX=1 on Linux; it never elevates itself. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
Owns the CC launcher (superclaude): starts Claude Code with Cairn's session contract, in its own memory-capped cgroup. WHY: Claude can OOM the box.
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

Each platform shell does two things, in order, before handing over: it elevates, then it runs Cairn's own Python on the launcher (on Windows `@python <path>\cairn ...`; on Linux the same without the @). Every decision after that is Python's; the shell holds no other logic beyond the fall-over above.

Elevation is the shell's, settled before Python starts, and nothing inside asks again. On Windows the shell runs in an elevated PowerShell. On Linux the shell sudoes the launch, with IS_SANDBOX=1 set so Claude Code accepts bypass permissions under root. WHY: the whole box is the sandbox, so elevating once at launch is simpler than elevating on request; IS_SANDBOX=1 is set on every box for that reason. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
Code that is no longer needed is deleted. Git history keeps it if we ever need it back.

A retirement checks its callers in the same act as the deletion: nothing imports the module being deleted, and nothing runs the command or path being deleted. A file that only names it (a fixture, a record, a charter) is not a caller. Nothing checks afterwards. Why? Naming is history; only a caller breaks, and a caller that comes later breaks loudly on its own. A standing proof that a thing stays gone is history kept as code.

`cairn codemother retire <path>...` does the deletion. It runs the proofs of the files that name the target, before and after moving it aside. A proof that turns red is a caller, and the target goes back. Why? Running a proof tells a caller from a mention; reading the text cannot.

Outline check: when a ticket is cast, the cheapest model reads it beside the outline sections it touches. A conflict, or an open question in those sections, becomes a [Q#n] at the outline line it bears on (0.6.2), and that open [Q#n] holds the ticket's build until it is answered. It reads the outline as it stands each time, so editing the outline costs nothing. WHY: a ticket that contradicts the outline builds something Akien did not intend, and the cheapest time to catch that is before the build. - CC

A ticket's plan is a plan, not a list of decisions: constraints, outcomes and resources. - Outcomes, not tasks: each is a claim a proof can check. An outcome hides the how. - Constraints: the bounds, and every how Akien is attached to (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel). - Order comes only from real dependencies (you can't test the bus envelope shape until the bus works), and those also set ticket order. - Resources: existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - A plan too big splits into tickets. Early steps can reshape later ones, so the whole is checked for coherence at the end. -amm

The reading: - A plan is three parts. Constraints: the bounds, plus every how Akien is attached to, carried verbatim (encapsulation, the bus as the only channel, ...): a how he states is a constraint. Then outcomes. Then resources. - An outcome is {n, claim, writes_to, reads, after: [n or a ticket id], via?}. The claim is falsifiable, one proof tooth per outcome. The falsifier's clauses merge into the outcomes; there is no separate falsifier list. Old clause n stays outcome n; outcomes made from decisions number after them. via (optional) names the tool or pattern to use, drawn from resources. - Order comes from after: only real dependencies, which also shape ticket order. Nothing invents them; list order is reading order only. - Resources: pre-existing machines, tools and design patterns, named when they need stating. - The migration is two steps. Mechanical, on every open ticket now: the plan moves to the new field with clause numbers kept, the trail moves whole to the log, by moves to the log. Judgement, when a ticket is next opened for build, never in bulk: each decision becomes an outcome or a constraint, then a coherence check (every step reads as current; a conflict moves to the log or is named). - CC inference: the mechanical step writes each old decision as an outcome numbered after the clauses, carrying its text and no claim; an outcome with no claim is awaiting judgement and holds BUILDME until the judgement step gives it a claim or moves it to constraints. - akienasus_cc_0 - During the change every reader accepts both shapes. Readers are censused first; one sibling ticket per reader component (RULE 1). - The cast door refuses an outcome with no falsifiable claim, and a plan of more than about 7 outcomes, naming children; each refusal is recorded so the ceiling can be tuned (the 7 is CC's guess). - The [?] markers go. - Tickets: aa3e9a70db47 is the migration (rehearsal); d421051bc1f7 is the hand-built worked example; each reader component has its sibling. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator -amm

Deleting code is about running code, not about the record of what happened. A retired path that something still CALLS is the defect; a retired path named by a record of what passed through (history, state, validations, verdicts, a measured fixture) is not. Requirements that police history are de-emphasized, because the aim is less history noise in front of Claude, not hidden history (Law 5).

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.

WHY: Law 8: nothing enters proven-space without a proof a hollow build couldn't pass, and the verdict must come from a hand the builder did not guide. A green cannot be self-granted. A machine under CodeMother, not a device: CodeMother does not build, so the tester inside her puts no builder between a build and its verdict, and nothing here needs its own process in the rack, since each proof run is its own process already.
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.

A red is first a question: is the code wrong, or is the tooth measuring the wrong thing? An LLM reads the work against the component's why, the tooth's why and CP1-CP6, because even the Laws rest finally on the core principles. Either the code or the tooth changes, and a tooth change carries that decision in the same act (corrosion, 17.11.6). A tooth a hollow build could pass is worthless at every tier (Law 8).
charter: compiles a component's bounded state from its history. WHY: state is compiled from the component's tickets, never hand-edited (Law 5). Held by CodeMother.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
Physics: the encapsulation_holds sieve in build_inspector, a device-path check. Code in device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo except a tool foo publishes. Inside one device nothing is checked.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.
